newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Outline of Stability and Growth Pact for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Outline of Stability and Growth Pact for EMU.

text.p: The new French government was expected on Monday to outline its views on the Stability and Growth Pact for a single European currency, due to be ratified by European Union leaders at a summit in Amsterdam next week.

The pact, provisionally agreed at an EU summit in Dublin in December, is designed to enforce fiscal discipline on countries which join its economic and monetary union (EMU), set to start on January 1, 1999.
As agreed in Dublin, the following steps would be taken against an EMU member government whose annual budget deficit rose above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

-- The European Commission, the EU's executive, would prepare an annual report on the offending country. The Commission would decide, "as a rule," that the country should be exempt from sanctions only if its GDP had suffered an annual fall of at least two percent.

-- A new Economic and Financial Committee would give an opinion on the Commission's report within two weeks. This opinion would be included in the Commission's recommendation to EU finance ministers about the government's finances.
The new committee would replace the monetary committee, which is made up of finance ministry and central bank officials.

-- EU ministers, the ultimate arbiters on sanctions, would take into account any evidence the government could provide "showing that an annual fall of real GDP of less than two percent is nevertheless exceptional in light of further supporting evidence."
A country could argue, for example, that the economic downturn was unusually abrupt or more severe than previous recessions.

-- If the ministers were not convinced the government has a good excuse for heavy borrowing, they would make recommendations on how it should curb its deficit, with clear deadlines for taking action -- four months.
-- The deficit should be cut back to the three percent limit by the following year "unless special circumstances are given."

-- If a government failed to take the EU's advice, the EU would order it to hand over a non-interest bearing deposit. This would happen at most 10 months after the budget overshoot was first identified.
-- The deposit would be converted into a fine after two years if the government's deficit was still considered excessive.

-- The initial deposit or fine would be 0.2 percent of GDP, with another 0.1 percent for every percentage point that the deficit goes over the three percent limit. The maximum fine would be 0.5 percent of GDP.
-- EU heads of state and government would issue a resolution urging "all parties to implement...the Stability and Growth Pact regulations strictly."

-- Under this resolution, if ministers did not act on a Commission recommendation, they would be urged to "state in writing the reasons which justify (their) decision not to act and to make public the votes cast by each member state."

-- Governments will pledge not to argue that their economic troubles are "exceptional" unless their economies are in a "severe recession." In deciding how severe the downturn is, governments will "as a rule" take a 0.75 percent decline in GDP as a guideline.
